title: Breaking Down the Prompt
summary: Spend four focused minutes decoding the issue and perspectives before you write.

sections.heading: Every Prompt Has the Same Skeleton
sections.body: ACT Writing prompts never change shape. You get a short paragraph introducing a debatable issue, three labeled perspectives that genuinely disagree, and a task line that repeats the same four requirements every single time. Because the format is fixed, you can walk in already knowing what you will be asked to do: state your own position, connect it to at least one other perspective, support it with reasoning and examples, and organize it clearly. That predictability is an advantage. The only unknown on test day is the topic itself, which means your reading time should go entirely toward understanding the specific disagreement in front of you, not toward figuring out what the task wants.

sections.heading: Find the Real Disagreement
sections.body: The three perspectives are not three flavors of the same opinion. They disagree about something specific, and your first job is to name it in your own words. Ask what question each perspective is actually answering. In a prompt about automation, one perspective may argue about whether automation is good, another about how fast it should happen, and a third about who should decide. Those are three different questions, which is exactly why the perspectives conflict. Once you can state the disagreement in a single sentence, you understand the prompt well enough to enter it. Students who skip this step usually end up summarizing all three views instead of arguing with them.

sections.heading: Annotate Fast and Physically
sections.body: Mark the test booklet as you read. Underline the key claim in each perspective, and write one word in the margin naming what that perspective values most: efficiency, fairness, tradition, freedom, safety. These one-word tags become the backbone of your analysis, because arguments between perspectives are almost always arguments between competing values rather than competing facts. Next, circle the strongest word in each perspective, usually an absolute like never, always, only, or must. Absolutes are where a perspective overreaches, and overreach is the easiest thing to argue against. Two minutes of marking gives you material for three body paragraphs.

sections.heading: Do Not Skip the Task Line
sections.body: The task line looks like boilerplate, and most students read past it. Read it anyway, because it is the scoring rubric written in plain language. It tells you to state your perspective, analyze the relationship between yours and at least one other, develop ideas with reasoning and examples, organize logically, and write in standard English. Those five demands correspond directly to the four domains graders score. If your essay does all five things visibly, you have earned a solid score before style enters the picture. Treat the task line as a checklist you will return to during your final read-through, not as decoration around the real prompt.

checklist: State the core disagreement between the perspectives in one sentence.
Tag each perspective with the single value it prioritizes.
Circle absolute words like never, always, and only that a perspective overreaches with.
Reread the task line and treat its five demands as your rubric.
Spend no more than four minutes total on prompt analysis.

title: Building a Thesis That Takes a Side
summary: A precise, arguable thesis is the single fastest way to raise your score.

sections.heading: Commit to a Position
sections.body: Graders reward a clear perspective, and the fastest way to lose points is to write an essay that likes everyone. A thesis such as both sides have good points announces that you will not argue, and an essay that does not argue cannot demonstrate analysis. Pick a side within the first two minutes, and pick it for strategic reasons rather than personal ones. The strongest choice is usually the position you can support with the most specific examples, not the one you privately believe. You are not being graded on sincerity. You are being graded on whether you can build and defend a case under time pressure.

sections.heading: You May Agree, Adopt, or Invent
sections.body: Three moves are all available and all score equally well. You can fully endorse one perspective and defend it. You can endorse one while noting a limit it fails to acknowledge, which is often the highest-scoring move because it shows independent judgment. Or you can advance a fourth position of your own, provided you still engage at least one of the given perspectives directly. What you may not do is stay outside the argument, describing what each perspective says without ever judging it. Summary is not analysis, and a well-organized summary of three views tends to land in the middle of the score range no matter how cleanly it is written.

sections.heading: Make the Thesis Specific Enough to Be Wrong
sections.body: A good test: could a reasonable person disagree with your thesis sentence? If not, it is too vague to argue. Phones can be distracting is not a thesis, because nobody disputes it. Phones should be inaccessible during instruction but available at lunch, because students need supervised practice rather than an eight-hour ban, is a thesis, because it names a policy, a boundary, and a reason. Specificity also makes the rest of the essay easier to write, since a precise claim tells you exactly which body paragraphs you owe the reader. A vague thesis leaves you inventing structure paragraph by paragraph while the clock runs.

sections.heading: Place It Where a Grader Will Find It
sections.body: Put your thesis at the end of your introduction, and state it in one or two sentences that could be lifted out and still make sense alone. Graders read quickly, often under a minute per essay on a first pass, and they are looking for your position early. Burying a strong claim in paragraph four means it may register as absent. It is also worth echoing the thesis briefly in your conclusion using different words, which reminds the reader what you argued without repeating the sentence verbatim. Consistency matters too: an essay whose conclusion quietly contradicts its introduction reads as unplanned.

checklist: Choose the side you can support best, not the side you personally hold.
Write a thesis a reasonable person could dispute.
Name a specific position, boundary, or condition rather than a general attitude.
Place the thesis at the end of the introduction.
Check that the conclusion still matches the thesis you started with.

title: Essay Structure and a Reusable Template
summary: One flexible five-part frame you can adapt to any prompt in under a minute.

sections.heading: Why a Template Helps
sections.body: Forty minutes is not enough time to invent an organizational scheme and generate content at the same time. A template removes the first job so you can spend your attention on the second. This is not the same as writing a formulaic essay: the frame is fixed, but the ideas inside it are entirely yours, and graders respond to the quality of thinking rather than to novel paragraph arrangements. Students who plan their structure in advance consistently finish, and finishing matters enormously. An incomplete essay with brilliant paragraphs scores lower than a complete essay with good ones, because organization and development are both scored on what actually appears on the page.

sections.heading: The Five-Part Frame
sections.body: Introduction: one or two sentences framing the issue in your own words, then your thesis. Body one: the perspective you disagree with most, presented fairly and then limited. Body two: another perspective, engaged the same way, showing where it is right and where it stops short. Body three: the positive case for your own position, with your strongest example. Conclusion: the strongest objection to your view, a brief answer to it, and a closing line that reframes rather than repeats. That final move, conceding and answering an objection near the end, is what separates upper-range essays from competent ones, and it costs only three or four sentences.

sections.heading: Adapting the Frame
sections.body: The template flexes. If you are running short on time, merge body two into body one and expand your own case, since your position matters more than exhaustive coverage. You are only required to engage one other perspective, not all three. If one perspective is clearly the weakest, dispatch it in three sentences and spend the saved time on the perspective closest to your own, where the interesting distinctions live. Order the perspectives deliberately, moving from most flawed to closest to correct, so the essay narrows toward your position instead of wandering. That ordering does organizational work by itself, and graders notice it.

sections.heading: Paragraphs That Do One Job
sections.body: Each body paragraph should open with a claim, not a summary. Compare Perspective One says automation is good with Perspective One correctly identifies the long-run pattern and wrongly assumes people live in the long run. The second version tells the reader what the paragraph will argue, which makes everything after it easier to follow. Then supply reasoning, then one developed example, then a sentence connecting the point back to your thesis. Four moves, roughly five to seven sentences. If a paragraph is trying to do two jobs, split it; if it is doing none, cut it and give the space to a paragraph that earns it.

sections.heading: Length and Proportion
sections.body: Aim for four to six paragraphs and roughly 400 to 600 words. Longer is not automatically better, but very short essays genuinely struggle, because development and support are graded on evidence that must physically be there. Watch your proportions: an introduction longer than four sentences is stealing time from your argument, and a conclusion that only restates the introduction is wasted space that could have held your counterargument. The bulk of your words belong in the body, and the single largest paragraph should usually be the one making your own case, since that is where a grader looks for your best thinking.

checklist: Sketch the five-part frame on scratch paper before writing.
Open each body paragraph with a claim rather than a summary.
Order perspectives from most flawed to closest to your own.
Reserve three or four sentences near the end for an objection and your answer.
Keep the introduction under four sentences.
Give your own position the longest paragraph.

title: Using Specific Evidence and Examples
summary: Specific, developed examples separate mid-range essays from high scorers.

sections.heading: Specific Beats Impressive
sections.body: Students often assume graders want famous historical examples, so they reach for the Industrial Revolution or a Supreme Court case they half remember. A vaguely recalled grand example is weaker than a precisely recalled ordinary one. Your history class, your part-time job, your town's closed factory, a policy your school changed last year: these are excellent evidence because you know the details, and details are what make an example persuasive. The test does not check your facts against a database, but a grader can tell instantly whether a writer actually knows what they are describing. Write about what you can describe in three concrete sentences.

sections.heading: Four Reliable Sources of Evidence
sections.body: You have more material than you think. Personal experience covers school, work, family, teams, and clubs. Observation covers your town, your neighborhood, and things you have watched change over time. Coursework covers history, science, literature, and current events from any class you have taken. Reasoning covers hypotheticals and analogies that illustrate a principle, which are fully legitimate evidence when the logic is sound. Most high-scoring essays mix at least two of these. Before you write, spend thirty seconds asking which of the four gives you the sharpest material for this particular topic, then commit to it rather than sampling all four thinly.

sections.heading: Develop, Do Not Just Name
sections.body: The most common failure is the drive-by example: a sentence naming something relevant, followed immediately by the next point. Development means three moves. State the example concretely, including a detail that could only come from someone who knows it. Explain what happened or what it shows. Then connect it explicitly to the claim it is supporting. That last move is the one students skip most, and it is where analysis actually lives. One example developed across four sentences is worth more than four examples named in a list, both because it demonstrates reasoning and because a list of names reads as padding.

sections.heading: Analogies Are Evidence Too
sections.body: A well-chosen analogy can prove a structural point faster than any statistic. Arguing that unrestricted phone access does not teach self-regulation, you might note that we do not teach driving by handing a teenager the keys and trusting the highway to instruct her. The analogy works because it isolates the principle at issue: demanding skills are taught in stages, under supervision. Choose analogies that share the actual structure of your argument rather than merely sounding clever, and state the shared structure explicitly in one sentence. An analogy left unexplained is a decoration; an analogy whose logic you name is an argument.

checklist: Choose examples you can describe in three concrete sentences.
Include one detail only someone familiar with the example would know.
Develop each example: state it, explain it, connect it to your claim.
Prefer one developed example over three named ones.
Name the shared logic whenever you use an analogy.

title: Handling Counterarguments
summary: Engaging the strongest opposing view is the clearest signal of real analysis.

sections.heading: Analysis Is Relationship, Not Summary
sections.body: The task line asks you to analyze the relationship between your perspective and at least one other. That word relationship is the whole assignment. Summarizing a perspective and then declaring that you disagree is not analysis; it is a report followed by a vote. Analysis means explaining what the other perspective gets right, what it assumes, where that assumption breaks down, and why your position handles the problem better. Essays that stall in the middle of the score range are usually well organized and grammatically clean but purely summary-based. Adding genuine engagement with an opposing view is the single most reliable upgrade available to most writers.

sections.heading: Steelman Before You Strike
sections.body: State the opposing perspective in its strongest form, ideally stronger than the prompt states it. This feels counterintuitive under time pressure, but it makes your rebuttal far more convincing, because a reader who sees you defeat a weak version assumes you could not defeat a strong one. Give the opposing view its best example and its most reasonable motive before you limit it. A useful sentence pattern: Perspective Two is right that compelled service produces hour-counting rather than generosity, and anyone who has watched students hunt for signatures knows it. Then turn. The concession costs one sentence and buys credibility for everything after it.

sections.heading: Turn on the Assumption, Not the Conclusion
sections.body: The strongest rebuttals attack a premise rather than contradicting a conclusion. Instead of writing that a perspective is wrong, identify what it must assume to be true and show why that assumption fails. A view that automation always creates better jobs assumes the new jobs appear in the same places, on the same timeline, for the same people. Naming that hidden assumption and showing it no longer holds is far more persuasive than asserting the opposite conclusion. This move also generates content quickly, because once you name an assumption, the example that undercuts it usually follows naturally.

sections.heading: Answer the Objection to Yourself
sections.body: The highest-scoring essays turn the same skill on their own position. Near the end, name the strongest objection to your argument, concede that it has real force, and explain why your position still holds. This is not weakness. It demonstrates that you understand the issue well enough to see your own limits, which is precisely the judgment graders reward. Keep it tight, three or four sentences: here is the fair objection, here is why the alternative costs more, here is what remains true. Reserve space for this in your outline so it does not get squeezed out by the clock.

checklist: State the opposing view in its strongest form before limiting it.
Identify the assumption a perspective depends on, then test it.
Explain what an opposing perspective gets right, not just what it misses.
Reserve three or four sentences near the end for an objection to your own view.
Answer that objection by comparing costs, not by dismissing it.

title: Timing and Revision in 40 Minutes
summary: A minute-by-minute plan that gets a complete, cleaned-up essay on the page.

sections.heading: A Minute-by-Minute Plan
sections.body: Minutes zero to four: read the prompt, mark the perspectives, and name the core disagreement. Minutes four to eight: choose your position, write your thesis on scratch paper, and jot the order of your body paragraphs with one example each. Minutes eight to thirty-four: write, without stopping to perfect sentences. Minutes thirty-four to forty: reread and clean up. Practice with this schedule until it feels automatic, and time yourself with a watch rather than guessing. Most students who run out of time did not write slowly; they spent twelve minutes deciding what to argue, which is a planning failure rather than a writing one.

sections.heading: Planning Is Not Optional
sections.body: Eight minutes of planning feels like a luxury when the clock is visible, and it is the best investment on the test. An outline as short as a thesis sentence plus four paragraph labels prevents the most expensive mistake in timed writing: discovering in paragraph three that your argument has changed, and either contradicting your introduction or spending minutes patching it. Planned essays also finish, because you always know what comes next. Write the outline on the booklet, not in your head, since working memory collapses under time pressure and a written plan takes ten seconds to reread when you lose your place.

sections.heading: Finish the Essay, Whatever Happens
sections.body: If you are at minute thirty and still in your second body paragraph, cut, do not rush. Skip the remaining body paragraph entirely and write your conclusion. A complete essay with three paragraphs scores meaningfully higher than an abandoned essay with four, because organization is judged on the whole and an essay stopping mid-thought reads as a failure of planning. Protect the conclusion the way you would protect the last question on a math section. Two solid sentences that state your position and answer one objection will always beat a fourth body paragraph that trails off when time is called.

sections.heading: What to Fix in Six Minutes
sections.body: Do not attempt a rewrite. Hunt for the errors that cost the most and take the least time to fix. First, check that your thesis is visible and that your conclusion agrees with it. Second, scan for the mechanical errors you personally repeat, which for most writers means apostrophes, its versus it's, your versus you're, and comma splices. Third, look for one vague sentence you can make specific, and one long tangled sentence you can split in two. Fourth, make sure paragraph breaks are unmistakable. Legibility counts as well: an unreadable word is a word that cannot earn credit.

sections.heading: Practice Under Real Conditions
sections.body: Write at least three full timed essays before test day, by hand, on lined paper, with a real forty-minute timer and no pausing. Handwriting is slower than typing, and discovering that difference on test day is an unpleasant surprise. After each practice essay, score yourself against the four domains and pick exactly one thing to improve next time, rather than trying to fix everything simultaneously. Keep a short list of your own recurring errors, since the same three or four mistakes tend to appear in every essay a person writes, and knowing yours turns the final six minutes into targeted proofreading.

checklist: Plan for eight minutes before writing a single sentence.
Write the outline on paper, not in your head.
Start the conclusion by minute thirty-four no matter where you are.
Proofread for your own repeat errors rather than reading generally.
Write at least three practice essays by hand with a real timer.
Keep a running list of the mistakes you personally repeat.
